topic: Why Australia's Beetle Fix Became a Toad Problem

claims.claim: In 1935, cane toads were brought to Australia to control Queensland's cane beetles.

claims.claim: The success of biological control of prickly-pear cactus by the introduced moth Cactoblastis cactorum in 1926 reinforced the consensus in Australia that biological control could solve the sugar industry's pest problems.
claims.support_quote: The highly successful control of exotic prickly-pear cactus by the introduced Argentinian moth Cactoblastis cactorum in 1926 added to the consensus that biological control was the answer to the sugar industry's woes.

claims.claim: The toads thrived in the wild but had little or no impact on cane beetles, which are today controlled by chemical pesticides.
claims.support_quote: The toads thrived in the wild but had little or no impact on cane beetles, which are today controlled by chemical pesticides.

claims.claim: Cane toads naturally generate potent bufadienolide toxins throughout their bodies, which act by stopping the heart of most animals that attempt to eat them.
claims.support_quote: Cane toads naturally generate potent toxins (bufodienolides) throughout their bodies, which act by stopping the heart of most animals that attempt to eat them.

claims.claim: The northern quoll is now listed as Endangered under the EPBC Act, with populations actively managed and toad-free island translocations used as a conservation measure.
claims.support_quote: The northern quoll is now listed as Endangered under state, national and international listings (IUCN Red List), and populations are being actively managed by various jurisdictions.

claims.claim: Cane toads have already caused widespread declines and local extinctions of several native predator species as they spread across northern Australia, and are recognised as one of Australia's most damaging invasive species.
claims.support_quote: Cane toads have already caused widespread declines and local extinctions of several native predator species as they have spread across northern Australia

claims.claim: COMPARABLE CASE: The small Indian mongoose was introduced to Hawai'i in 1883 by the sugar industry to control rats in sugarcane fields.
claims.support_quote: were originally introduced to Hawai'i Island in 1883 by the sugar industry to control rats in sugarcane fields on Maui, Moloka'i and O'ahu

claims.claim: COMPARABLE CASE: The mongoose introduction was misguided because, while rodents form much of its diet, its negative impact on native birds and other animals outweighed its minor impact on rats.
claims.support_quote: The introduction of mongoose was misguided- while rodents make up a large portion of the mongooses' diet, their substantial negative impact on other desirable birds, insects, and animals outweighs their minor impact on rat populations.

claims.claim: COMPARABLE CASE: Because mongooses are active by day and rats at night, the two rarely encountered each other, and the mongoose introduction did little to control rats while instead threatening ground-nesting native birds such as the nene and petrels.
claims.support_quote: now both mongoose and rats threaten populations of native birds, particularly ground-nesting species like nēnē and petrels

claims.claim: COMPARABLE CONTRAST: The vast majority of biological control efforts in Hawai'i have succeeded, such as prickly-pear cactus now checked by predatory insects and a fungus, showing that properly tested biocontrol can work.
claims.support_quote: The vast majority of biological control efforts in Hawaii have been successful

unverified_claims.claim: In August 1935, 2400 cane toads were released in the Gordonvale area near Cairns, Queensland.
unverified_claims.support_quote: in August of 1935, 2400 cane toads were released in the Gordonvale area, near Cairns in Queensland

unverified_claims.claim: The cane toads introduced to Australia were brought from Hawaii, where they had been introduced from Puerto Rico.
unverified_claims.support_quote: Cane toads are native to Central and South America, but the toads introduced to Australia were brought from Hawaii.

unverified_claims.claim: In 1932 Bureau of Sugar Experiment Stations plant pathologist Arthur Bell learned of the apparent success of Bufo marinus against cane beetles at a conference in Puerto Rico, and reported on it.
unverified_claims.support_quote: In 1932 Bureau of Sugar Experiment Stations plant pathologist Arthur Bell attended a conference in Puerto Rico where he learned of and then reported on the apparent success of the American toad

unverified_claims.claim: Lobbying by cane farmers led to the 1900 establishment of the Bureau of Sugar Experiment Stations, whose entomologists worked on the cane beetle problem for years before the toad was introduced, initially experimenting with chemical control methods.
unverified_claims.support_quote: Lobbying by cane farmers led to the establishment in 1900 of the Bureau of Sugar Experiment Stations, staffed by entomologists who worked on the cane beetle problem for many years before the introduction of the toad.

unverified_claims.claim: The entomologists hoped the cane toads would eat the cane beetles but had not tested whether this was likely, nor studied how the toads might affect the Australian environment.
unverified_claims.support_quote: The entomologists hoped that the cane toads would eat the cane beetles, but, surprisingly, they hadn't tested if this was likely to happen.

unverified_claims.claim: Retired NSW Chief Entomologist Walter Froggatt publicly warned that the cane toad might become as great a pest as the rabbit or prickly-pear cactus.

unverified_claims.claim: Analyses confirm sugar production did not increase significantly after the toads were released, possibly because toads reduced predation on beetle pests by consuming native predators (ants), poisoning others (varanid lizards), and increasing abundances of crop-eating rodents.
unverified_claims.support_quote: Our analyses confirm that sugar production did not increase significantly after the anurans were released

unverified_claims.claim: The cane toad was first declared a problem species in 1950.
unverified_claims.support_quote: The toad was first declared a problem species in 1950.

unverified_claims.claim: Cane toads are now moving westward at an estimated 40 to 60 km per year.
unverified_claims.support_quote: they are now moving westward at an estimated 40 to 60 km per year

unverified_claims.claim: In Australia there are no specific predators or diseases that control cane toads, and there is no broadscale way to control the pest.
unverified_claims.support_quote: In Australia there are no specific predators or diseases that control cane toads.

unverified_claims.claim: In 2005 the biological effects, including lethal toxic ingestion, caused by cane toads were listed as a key threatening process under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999.
unverified_claims.support_quote: In 2005, The biological effects, including lethal toxic ingestion, caused by Cane Toads (Bufo marinus) was listed as a key threatening process under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999.

unverified_claims.claim: A single pathway—lethal toxic ingestion of toads by frog-eating predators—is the major mechanism of impact, though its magnitude varies dramatically among predator taxa and across space and time.
unverified_claims.support_quote: a single pathway-lethal toxic ingestion of toads by frog-eating predators-is the major mechanism of impact, but that the magnitude of impact varies dramatically among predator taxa

unverified_claims.claim: No native species has gone extinct as a result of toad invasion, and some taxa severely impacted recover within a few decades via aversion learning and adaptive change.
unverified_claims.support_quote: No native species have gone extinct as a result of toad invasion

unverified_claims.claim: Local populations of northern quolls typically collapse soon after an area is colonised by cane toads.
unverified_claims.support_quote: Local populations of northern quolls typically collapse soon after an area is colonised by cane toads.

unverified_claims.claim: Cane toads occupy about 60% of the prior range of the northern quoll and are likely to occur across most of the rest within the next 10-20 years.
unverified_claims.support_quote: Cane toads now occupy about 60% of the prior range of northern quolls, and are likely to occur across most of the rest of that range in the next 10-20 years.
